summary: The article describes the new Sphere venue in Las Vegas, a US$2.3b entertainment space with the highest-resolution LED screen ever made, beam-forming audio and haptics, which opened with a U2 show. It compares Sphere to ABBA Voyage in London and quotes Stufish's Ric Lipson on how such venues could make concerts more plug-and-play and sustainable. It also notes the venue's cinema use, including Darren Aronofsky's Postcard From Earth, and its roots in 1950s immersive film technology.
one_line: Las Vegas's US$2.3b Sphere, launched with U2, offers an immersive screen-and-sound venue that could reshape concerts, alongside ABBA's London arena.
key_facts: The Sphere in Las Vegas has an interior 16K x 16K spherical video surface, the highest-resolution LED screen ever made, with 268,435,456 pixels.
The Sphere's exterior is covered by 1.2 million hockey-puck-sized LEDs.
The venue has 157,000 ultra-directional speakers using "beam-forming acoustics", plus "infrasound haptics" that shape soundwaves into vibrations and air-pressure waves.
In the U2 show, the audience journeys through environments referencing the band's creative history; Stufish partner Ric Lipson, Es Devlin and Brian Eno collaborated on the project.
Stufish also worked on the ABBA Arena in London, the Queen's Platinum Jubilee, and tours for Beyoncé, Jay-Z, Michael Bublé, Elton John and Madonna.
ABBA pushes its effects out toward the audience, while Sphere more wholly and subtly envelops them.
Lipson says that because everyone gets their own sound feed in the Sphere, everybody hears an equal volume, so the sound may be better than anywhere.
Lipson says Adele's show at Caesar's Palace takes about a week to load out, whereas the Sphere's planners are considering multiple spheres so shows could move from sphere to sphere.
In cinema mode the Sphere adds artificial wind and scents paired to key moments such as rocket launches or wild storms.
Cinerama in the 1950s used three synchronised 35mm projectors and reached only 146 degrees, versus the Sphere's 270-degree view.
Darren Aronofsky's Postcard From Earth is a 50-minute 18K film shot with an 18K Big Sky camera, with sequences shot in Greece, India, Mexico and the USA.
The Big Sky camera delivers an image about 40 times greater in resolution than a 4K television screen.
Lipson and Williams caution that storytelling and the artist-audience relationship remain the key draw despite the scale of the technology.
